newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka army launches recruitment drive.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka army launches recruitment drive.

text.p: The Sri Lankan army has launched a major recruitment drive following the recent upsurge in the war with separatist Tamil Tiger rebels.
"Our resources have weakened considerably and we want to recruit tens of thousands of soldiers," a military spokesman said on Sunday.
He said more than 7,000 local government officials were involved in the nationwide programme and the military was running daily recruitment advertisements in local newspapers.
"We are now consolidating military positions in front areas and we will have to wait until we have enough resources before staging a major offensive," a senior military official told Reuters.

The military balance has remained largely unchanged since the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) handed the military its worst setback in the 13-year war in July when they overran a strategic army base.
The army launched an offensive soon after the LTTE wiped out the northeastern Mullaitivu camp killing or capturing almost its entire garrison of 1,400 men.
But the army's push, advancing south from the northern peninsula of Jaffna, has been stalled around the town of Kilinochchi, a gateway to the rebels' jungle stronghold of Wanni.
"About 30 percent of the military's full strength has been kept in Jaffna since its recapture of the peninsula last April," an Asian diplomat said.
"The government forces have also been weakened after a series of major offensives against the LTTE," he said.

The Tigers, fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in the country's north and east, had ruled Jaffna as a mini-state for almost a decade with their own administration, courts and police.
Western diplomats said the current lull in the ethnic war indicated the army had exhausted itself after a thrust towards Kilinochchi in July.
"I'm not surprised to see a lull in activity," said a Western diplomat. "The Kilinochchi offensive was hastily planned."
Government forces have remained on the outskirts of Kilinochchi for the past month.

"We will consolidate our positions until we have enough resources. We would like to clear the jungle area but we need a lot of resources to do that," an army brigadier said, asking not to be identified.
The government says more than 50,000 people have died in the war which began in 1983.
